extracted.intended_audience: general newspaper readers interested in WWII news and Allied activities
extracted.subtask_description: Contemporary newspaper coverage of World War II events, including battlefield reports, air raids, Allied broadcasting policy, and medical rehabilitation programs. Focus is on factual reporting of operations and descriptions of official policies and practices.

rubrics_metrics.name: Policy of understatement in Allied broadcasts
rubrics_metrics.description: There is a deliberate policy of understatement: Allied victories are described in the simplest terms, with a policy of understatement rather than the exaggeration and bragging of Axis spokesmen.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The American station and its staff 'strip the program to essentials which are easily understood and quickly grasped.' Announcers speak plainly and almost in a monotone to avoid excitement or sensationalism.

rubrics_metrics.name: Avoidance of bombast; present bad news with good
rubrics_metrics.description: No bombast — Extreme care is used to avoid any extravagant claims of damage or other occurrences within enemy territory; the station tells the unfavorable as well as the favorable news.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This policy 'eliminates the danger of having listeners lose faith in the station's credibility.' Announcers avoid exaggeration and present developments in a calm, matter-of-fact manner.

rubrics_metrics.name: Avoid attempts to excite listeners
rubrics_metrics.description: Announcers avoid any attempt to excite the listener (e.g., whistles, showy delivery); broadcasts are deliberately plain and restrained.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Programs are stripped to essentials; signature tunes or short familiar snippets may be used sparingly ('Over There' is used because it is widely known), but musical accompaniments and other commercial trappings are generally dispensed with.

rubrics_metrics.name: Minimize editorializing and vilification
rubrics_metrics.description: Editorializing on the news is minimized and 'Axis leaders are never vilified' in routine broadcasts.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Notable exceptions are limited (e.g., warnings to civilian populations). The goal is to maintain credibility and avoid inflaming audiences or provoking premature demonstrations.

rubrics_metrics.name: Careful avoidance of extravagant claims / confirmation discipline
rubrics_metrics.description: Extreme care is used to avoid extravagant claims of damage or events inside enemy territory; claims are checked to avoid misinformation.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The station avoids broadcasting unconfirmed or exaggerated reports so listeners will not lose faith; examples include cautious phrasing about damage and corroboration by reconnaissance photographs when possible.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use of multiple languages and rebroadcasts
rubrics_metrics.description: United Nations Radio broadcasts news daily in four languages—French, German, Italian and English—and rebroadcasts BBC programs for broader reach.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Programming strategy includes language-targeted news and use of established Allied outlets (BBC) to reach Axis-occupied populations effectively.

rubrics_metrics.name: Technical reach and transmission power
rubrics_metrics.description: Use of a powerful transmitter (the 50,000-watt medium-wave United Nations Radio) to reach Nazi-occupied Europe.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: High-power medium-wave transmission is part of the strategy to ensure penetration into occupied territories and to maintain a steady flow of reliable information.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use of warnings and practical advice for occupied populations
rubrics_metrics.description: Broadcasts include practical warnings to occupied-country civilians (for example, to stay away from targets) rather than sensational appeals.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: These warnings are presented plainly alongside other news to reduce civilian casualties and to avoid encouraging premature public demonstrations.

rubrics_metrics.name: Rehabilitation center classification (four stages)
rubrics_metrics.description: Patients in the rehabilitation center are graded into four classes: Class D can barely toddle; Class C can go on a 5-mile hike and do some exercises but not run or jump; Class B can run and jump; Class A is about ready to return to duty.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Most arrive in Class C; classifications are reviewed weekly and patients are regraded up or down as they progress.

rubrics_metrics.name: Referral and objective of rehabilitation program
rubrics_metrics.description: The rehabilitation center is a link between surgical care and full military function: patients are referred from station or general hospitals to be restored to full use and return to duty.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The program addresses both battle casualties (15–18%) and accident victims; objectives are individualized recovery and restoring soldiers to military fitness rather than merely ending hospital status.

rubrics_metrics.name: Individualized, progressive physical training and equipment adaptation
rubrics_metrics.description: Rehabilitation uses individualized exercises (pulley weights, ship's-wheel exercises, rope exercises, exercise bikes, homemade devices) tailored to each patient's needs to rebuild strength and function.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Patients follow daily regimens, progress is measured by weekly reclassification, and homemade or adapted equipment is employed to meet specific rehabilitation goals (e.g., restoring ankle, shoulder, back strength).
